examples.question_text: A local news report claims: “$78\%$ of residents want more tennis courts.” The survey questioned $250$ people attending a tennis tournament. Explain the sampling problem and state a conclusion the survey supports.
examples.solution_text:
Tournament attendees may be more interested in tennis than residents generally. Residents who did not attend were not represented by this sampling method.
The survey supports: “$78\%$ of the tournament attendees surveyed wanted more tennis courts.” It does not establish the percentage among all residents.

examples.question_text: An advertisement claims: “Our language app improves fluency.” Its study recorded only how many lessons users completed. Identify what was measured and explain whether it supports the claim.
examples.solution_text:
The study measured lessons completed, not fluency. Completing lessons does not itself show that users became more fluent.
The claim is unsupported by this measurement. Comparable assessments of fluency before and after use would help measure change, but would not alone establish that the app caused it.

examples.question_text: A report finds that towns with more libraries have more university graduates. Its headline says: “Libraries cause university success.” Explain the fault and give another possible explanation.
examples.solution_text:
The report shows an association between two counts, which alone does not establish causation.
Larger towns may have both more libraries and more graduates because they have more residents. Population size is a possible explanation, but the supplied report does not test it.

examples.question_text: An online article states only: “$73\%$ of commuters favour cheaper train fares.” Give two questions that would help you judge the report and explain why each matters.
examples.solution_text:
“How many commuters were surveyed?” Under comparable, appropriate sampling, larger samples generally have less chance variation. A large sample can still be biased.
“How were they selected?” The selection method helps establish whether respondents represent the commuters named in the claim. For example, a poll shared only by a train-users’ campaign group may miss other commuters.

examples.question_text: A reusable-bottle manufacturer funds a study reporting that its bottles last longer than competitors’ bottles. Explain how a reader should assess the report.
examples.solution_text:
The manufacturer benefits from a favourable result, so its funding is a reason to examine the testing and reporting carefully. Funding alone does not prove the result false.
Check which bottles were tested, whether all received the same treatment and whether all results were reported. Look for independent testing using comparable methods.

examples.question_text: A radio station invites listeners to vote online about closing a shopping street to traffic. Of $7200$ voters, $65\%$ support closure. The station announces: “The city supports closure.” Explain the problem and rewrite the claim.
examples.solution_text:
Voters chose whether to participate. People with strong views may be more likely to vote, and the station’s listeners may differ from city residents generally. The large vote count does not remove these sampling concerns.
A supported claim is: “$65\%$ of the $7200$ people who chose to vote in the station’s poll supported closure.”

examples.question_text: A library emails $6000$ members a survey. It receives $300$ replies, of which $84\%$ rate its opening hours suitable. Its report says: “$84\%$ of members approve our hours.” Calculate the response rate and explain how the claim should change.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}\text{Response rate} &= \frac{300}{6000}\times100\% \\ &= 5\%\end{align*}$
The other $5700$ members supplied no ratings. Respondents may differ from non-respondents; the report does not establish the direction or size of any resulting bias.
The claim should say: “$84\%$ of the $300$ members who replied rated our opening hours suitable.”

examples.question_text: A report says complaints rose from $4$ to $8$ in a year, among $20\,000$ customers. Its headline reads: “Complaints double.” Evaluate the headline using the counts and the customer total.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}\text{Ratio of complaint counts} &= \frac{8}{4} \\ &= 2 \\ \text{Current complaints as a percentage of customers} &= \frac{8}{20\,000}\times100\% \\ &= 0.04\%\end{align*}$
The complaint count did double, so the headline is arithmetically correct. The absolute increase was $4$ complaints.
Including the counts and customer total gives useful context. These figures alone do not establish the importance or cause of the increase.

examples.question_text: A drink advertisement claims: “Luma has the least sugar.” It compares $5$ g in a $150$ mL serve of Luma with $8$ g in a $300$ mL serve of another drink. Compare the sugar per $100$ mL, to two decimal places, and evaluate the claim.
examples.solution_text:
Compare equal volumes.
$\begin{align*}\text{Luma sugar per }100\text{ mL} &= \frac{5}{150}\times100 \\ &\approx 3.33\text{ g} \\ \text{Other drink sugar per }100\text{ mL} &= \frac{8}{300}\times100 \\ &\approx 2.67\text{ g}\end{align*}$
Luma has less sugar in the stated serve, but more sugar in the same volume. The unequal serves do not support the headline. Comparing only two drinks also cannot establish that Luma has the least sugar of all drinks.

Visits fell from $360$ in February to $300$ in March, contradicting “every month”.
A supported alternative is: “Pool visits increased overall from $240$ in January to $400$ in April, with a fall in March.” The graph does not establish a longer-term trend.

examples.question_text: A council is considering a new parking system. A supplier’s report states that “$89\%$ of users find it convenient”, but gives no sample size, selection method or exact survey question. State what the council should do before using the report to decide.
examples.solution_text:
Ask for the sample size, target population, selection method, response rate and exact question. These details help assess what the percentage measures and whom it can describe.
The supplier has a commercial interest, so also seek independent evidence of performance in comparable locations. Until the missing details are supplied and assessed, the percentage provides insufficient support for the council’s decision.

examples.question_text: A survey asks: “Do you agree that our unsafe roads urgently need the protection of more speed cameras?” Of $800$ respondents, $74\%$ agree. Identify a wording concern, suggest a neutral question and state what the reported percentage establishes.
examples.solution_text:
The wording describes the roads as unsafe and presents cameras as urgently needed protection before asking for agreement. This may influence responses.
A more neutral question is: “Do you support installing more speed cameras on these roads?”
The $74\%$ describes agreement with the original question among those respondents. The report does not measure how much the wording affected answers or establish the result a neutral question would produce.

examples.question_text: A report finds that $57\%$ of surveyed shoppers prefer Store A and $43\%$ prefer Store B. Its headline reads: “Almost everyone chooses Store A.” Calculate the percentage-point gap and evaluate the headline.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}\text{Percentage-point gap} &= 57-43 \\ &= 14\end{align*}$
Store A leads by $14$ percentage points, but $43\%$ of respondents prefer Store B. A majority prefers Store A; this is not almost everyone.
A supported headline is: “$57\%$ of surveyed shoppers prefer Store A.” The gap is measured in percentage points, not as a $14\%$ relative increase.

examples.question_text: A property report says: “Typical prices have risen $50\%$ since $2020$.” It lists typical prices of $\$480\,000$ in $2018$, $\$360\,000$ in $2020$ and $\$540\,000$ in $2025$. The $2020$ value was the lowest in the decade. Calculate the percentage rise to $2025$ from each listed starting year and explain how choosing $2020$ shapes the headline.
examples.solution_text:
Measure each rise relative to its starting price.
$\begin{align*}\text{Rise from }2020 &= \frac{540\,000-360\,000}{360\,000}\times100\% \\ &= 50\%\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}\text{Rise from }2018 &= \frac{540\,000-480\,000}{480\,000}\times100\% \\ &= 12.5\%\end{align*}$
Both comparisons end at the same $2025$ price. The lower starting price in $2020$ gives a larger increase relative to the baseline, producing the larger reported percentage rise.
The $50\%$ is correct for the selected period, but starting at the decade’s lowest price flatters the growth. Showing prices across the decade would provide context; these figures do not establish why the starting year was chosen.

examples.question_text: A council must choose between two litter-reduction campaigns. Report A, published by the company selling Campaign A, says that $86\%$ of surveyed residents believe the campaign reduced litter. It gives no sample size or selection method. Report B, published by a university, says that $69\%$ of $420$ monitored street sections met a litter-cleanliness standard after Campaign B. It identifies the streets, inspection dates and standard used. Explain why the council cannot choose the more effective campaign by comparing these percentages, and state what evidence it should request before deciding.
examples.solution_text:
Report A measures residents’ opinions about litter reduction. Report B measures the proportion of monitored street sections meeting a cleanliness standard. These are different outcomes with different denominators, so $86\%$ and $69\%$ cannot be directly compared to rank the campaigns’ effectiveness.
Report B provides more checkable details, but meeting a standard after a campaign does not show how much litter changed or that the campaign caused a change. Report A’s commercial publisher is a reason to scrutinise its methods, not proof that its finding is false.
Ask Report A’s publisher for the sample size, selection method and exact question. Ask both publishers for litter measurements before and after each campaign, using the same measure, inspection procedure and time period in comparable locations. Also seek evidence that any reduction can reasonably be attributed to the campaigns rather than other influences, such as changes in street cleaning.
The council should assess this comparable outcome evidence before deciding; neither supplied percentage establishes which campaign is more effective.

examples.derivation: Sampling tournament attendees can overrepresent interest in tennis. The 78% describes surveyed attendees; the sampling method does not establish residents’ preferences.
Lesson completion is the recorded variable; fluency is not measured. Before-and-after fluency assessments could measure change, but change alone would not establish causation.

An association between library counts and graduate counts does not establish causation. Larger populations could produce both larger counts; the solution correctly presents this as an untested possibility.

Sample size informs chance variation under comparable appropriate sampling. Recruitment determines potential representativeness. Both requested questions are relevant, and the solution correctly distinguishes size from bias.
Commercial funding creates an interest in favourable findings without proving falsity. Comparable testing conditions, complete reporting and independent evidence are relevant checks.

Voluntary online voting creates a self-selected sample; station listeners need not represent city residents. The 65% describes the 7200 poll participants. Neither the participation count nor the supplied recruitment establishes citywide support. The rewritten claim correctly limits its conclusion to participants. No diagram or calculation is required.
300/6000 × 100% = 5%; 6000 − 300 = 5700 non-respondents. The 84% describes replying members. Their missing counterparts’ ratings and any bias direction remain unknown.
8/4 = 2, so complaints doubled. The increase is 8 − 4 = 4 complaints, and 8/20000 × 100% = 0.04%. These establish numerical context without establishing cause or importance.

Luma contains 5/150 times 100 = 3.333... g per 100 mL; the other drink contains 8/300 times 100 = 2.666... g. Rounded values are 3.33 g and 2.67 g. Luma is higher on an equal-volume comparison, and two drinks cannot establish an all-drinks minimum.

The bar coordinates independently give January 240, February 360, March 300 and April 400 visits. February to March falls by 60, contradicting uninterrupted monthly growth; January to April increases by 160, supporting the stated overall increase. The Visits title is now at x=-1.5, separate from tick labels anchored at x=-0.12, with left space reserved to x=-1.8. The repair preserves values, black unshaded marks, the 10 pt title and 8.5 pt ticks. Actual rendered clearance remains for visual verification.

The reported percentage lacks the information needed to assess measurement and population scope. Requesting sampling and wording details, then comparable independent performance evidence, appropriately supports the council’s decision.

The original question supplies favourable premises about cameras before requesting agreement. The proposed question removes those premises. The 74% establishes agreement among respondents to the original wording, without quantifying a wording effect.
57 − 43 = 14 percentage points. A 57% majority alongside 43% preferring the alternative does not support 'almost everyone'. The replacement headline accurately names surveyed shoppers.

From 2020, (540000−360000)/360000 times 100% equals 50%. From 2018, (540000−480000)/480000 times 100% equals 12.5%. The lower baseline produces the larger rise to the same endpoint; the figures do not establish the publisher's motive.

86% measures residents’ opinions, whereas 69% measures street sections meeting a standard. Different outcomes and denominators prevent ranking effectiveness directly. Comparable before-and-after litter measurements and evidence addressing other influences are appropriate requests; neither funding nor post-campaign attainment alone establishes effectiveness.
